capitals.name: Pratishthana (Paithan)
capitals.note: The page calls Pratishthana the main early capital and lists Amaravati/Dharanikota, Pauni and Junnar as later, court or inscriptional seats without giving years; Dhavalikar thinks the original capital was Junnar. Gautamiputra is 'Lord of Benakataka' (Nashik region or Pauni). Ptolemy places a Pulumavi capital at Pratishthana c. 140 CE.

keyframe_review.note: 535,339 km2 (page gives no infobox area, so no ratio). CONTESTED, kept as Cliopatria's: the page says scholars date the start of rule anywhere from 271 BCE to 30 BCE and that the mainstream view is that rule began in 'the late 2nd century BCE'. The first dated king is Kanha (c. 100-70 BCE), who 'extended the kingdom up to Nashik in the west', yet this shape already reaches the west coast, the Narmada and Vidarbha, which the page credits to Kanha and Satakarni I. Expect the early extent to be overdrawn; the maurya-empire dossier hands the Deccan to this state in -225 and is kept consistent.

The shape matches the extent of Gautamiputra's Nashik prashasti ('from Malwa and Saurashtra in the north to Krishna River in the south', 'from Konkan in the west to Vidarbha (Berar) in the east'), but the page dates him anywhere from 60-85 CE to 106-130 CE, and says 'it is not clear' he effectively controlled all of it. The shape stands for 106-123 although the Western Satraps page says Nahapana 'held sway over Malwa, Southern Gujarat, and Northern Konkan' and 'occupied portions of the Satavahana Empire in western and central India', and dates a Kshatrapa defeat of the Satavahanas to 105-106 CE (Nasik Cave 10) without naming land; Nahapana's own reign is dated 24-70, 66-71 or 119-124 CE on the pages, so no loss is drawn and the 124 gain repeats land Cliopatria never removed.

region.text: the Deccan plateau (Maharashtra, Telangana, northern Karnataka, southern Madhya Pradesh) as Cliopatria draws the first shape

ledger.note: Dynasty begins in the Deccan. The page says scholars date the start of rule anywhere from 271 BCE to 30 BCE and that the mainstream view puts it in 'the late 2nd century BCE'. -225 is Cliopatria's year, matching maurya-empire's -225 loss of the Deccan; the page is silent on a single year.

-31: Satakarni I's conquest of Western Malwa (Ujjain). 'He seems to have conquered Western Malwa region from the Shungas' (Satakarni I page, no year); his reign is 'generally dated to 70-60 BCE', 187-177 BCE by some and 88-42 BCE 'most recently'; the Satavahana page has him conquer 'western Malwa, Anupa (Narmada valley) and Vidarbha', taking advantage of the turmoil caused by Greek invasions. The year is Cliopatria's: Ujjain (23.18N) lies in no Satavahana, Shunga or Kanva shape before -31, and the Indo-Scythians page has Vikrama retake Ujjain from the Indo-Scythians in 58 BCE, which a 70-60 BCE conquest from the Shungas would contradict, so the page's span is not drawn. The counterpart is nobody: the Shungas ended in -73 and the shunga-empire dossier has no loss. Confidence 1. (The earlier version dated this -70 against the Shungas and said 'the lands lie inside Cliopatria's shape from -225', which is false for Ujjain.)

region.text: Kanva land in Central India (Vidisha and the cells added in 27 BCE), without Chhattisgarh

ledger.note: 28 BCE: the Satavahanas end the Kanva dynasty. 'According to the Puranas, their dynasty was brought to an end by the Satavahanas in 28 BCE'; the page calls it 'a localised event in Central India' and notes the lack of numismatic and archaeological evidence for the killing of the last Kanva by Balipuccha. The region is the cells Cliopatria adds in -27. The Satavahana page adds that Satakarni II 'captured eastern Malwa from the Shungas' (he ruled 56 years; Ollett argues for a single Satakarni, ca. 88-42 BCE), and the Kanva page says the Kanvas 'allowed the kings of the Shunga dynasty to continue to rule in obscurity in a corner of their former dominions' and calls Vidisha the capital of 'later Shunga rulers': Cliopatria draws Vidisha in the Satavahana shape only from -27, so this event carries the eastern Malwa capture (the earlier separate -50 entry duplicated it and was dropped in the sa-02-b repair). Chhattisgarh is left out: the mahameghavahana-dynasty holds it until 109.

early 2nd century CE: Gautamiputra Satakarni takes South Kosala. 'South Kosala was later conquered by Gautamiputra Satakarni of the Satavahana dynasty' 'in the early part of the 2nd century CE and remained in their possession up to the second half of the 2nd century CE' (Mahameghavahana page, no year; the sentence has no citation). 110 is the rounded year of the mirror loss in mahameghavahana-dynasty; the Gautamiputra page dates his reign between 60-85 and 106-130 CE. The page adds that the Meghas later 'regained their suzerainty over South Kosala' in the 2nd-3rd century CE, undated, so the Satavahana shapes of 161-215 that keep Chhattisgarh are probably too large (see notes). The Gautamiputra page does not mention South Kosala.

region.text: Aparanta (northern Konkan), Akaravanti (Malwa) and the Nashik-Pune country, from which Gautamiputra 'drove the Sakas'

ledger.note: c. 124 CE: Gautamiputra Satakarni defeats Nahapana. Most historians now agree (Gautamiputra page) that Gautamiputra and Nahapana were contemporaries and that Gautamiputra defeated Nahapana; Dhavalikar dates it c. 124 CE (his 18th regnal year), Fynes after 71 CE, Bhandare 78 CE. His Nashik inscription calls him 'king of Asika, Asaka, Mulaka, Suratha, Kukura, Aparanta, Anupa, Vidabha, Akaravanti' and he 'uprooted the Kshaharata (or Khagarata) family'; the Gautamiputra page does not say which lands came from Nahapana. The Western Satraps page says Nahapana 'held sway over Malwa, Southern Gujarat, and Northern Konkan, from Bharuch to Sopara' and that 'Gautamiputra drove the Sakas from Malwa and Western Maharashtra', which gives the region. Sa-02-b repair: Vidarbha was removed (no page ties it to Nahapana; the Satavahana page credits it to Satakarni I) and the confidence lowered from 2 to 1: the gain repeats land Cliopatria never removed (the -27..126 shapes hold all of it) and no loss to the Kshaharatas is entered, because no page dates one consistently: the Satavahana page has the Western Kshatrapas extend their influence 'during 15-40 CE', the Western Satraps page dates a Kshatrapa defeat of the Satavahanas to 105-106 CE (Nasik Cave 10) without naming land, and Nahapana's own reign is dated 24-70, 66-71 or 119-124 CE.

region.text: the territories previously held by Nahapana, except Poona and Nasik (Kardamaka/Rudradaman gain)

ledger.note: c. 127 CE: Kshatrapa Rudradaman takes back Nahapana's former lands. 'It is possible that by the end of his reign, Gautamiputra lost some of his territory to the Kardamakas'; Rudradaman 'regained all the former territories previously held by Nahapana' except 'the southern territory of Poona and Nasik' (Rudradaman page, r. 130-150). 127 is the end of Gautamiputra's reign in Higham's chronology (103-127) and Cliopatria's year. Sa-02-b repair: Nasik is kept out of the region (Poona lies inside the 127 shape already); the Western Satraps page also says 'Rudradaman regained all the previous territories held by Nahapana'.

c. 154 CE: Aparanta returns to the Satavahanas. Rudradaman 'conceded the country of Aparanta to Vashishtiputra Satakarni' as dowry (Rudradaman page, undated; the daughter's marriage ended the hostilities). 154 is Cliopatria's year; the page gives none. Vashishtiputra Satakarni's own page dates his reign 158-165 CE, does not mention Aparanta or a dowry and gives no year for the marriage, so 154 stays Cliopatria's year at confidence 1.

region.text: the southern dominions of the Western Satraps: Aparanta and the eastern Central Provinces

ledger.note: c. 184 CE: Yajna Sri Satakarni recovers the south of the Western Satraps' lands. He 'defeated the Western Satraps and reconquered their southern regions in western and central India' and 'not only ruled Aparanta, but probably also the eastern part of the Central Provinces' (Majumdar). The page gives only reign variants (c. 152-181, 165-195, 170-199, 174-203); 184 is Cliopatria's year. The Western Satraps page says Yajna Sri (170-199 CE) 'defeated the Western Satraps in the late 2nd century CE, thereby reconquering their southern regions'; the Yajna Sri page also gives no year.

region.text: the northern parts of the kingdom, near Nashik

ledger.note: c. 203 CE: the Abhiras take the north around Nashik. 'The Abhiras captured the northern parts of the kingdom' in Yajna Satakarni's last years (Satavahana page, no year). 203 is the end of the longest reign variant (174-203) and matches 'Established: 203' in the Abhira dynasty infobox (Abhira page, read 2026-10-19), which gives no year for the seizure and has the branch come to power 'after the demise of the Satavahanas in the Nasik region'; the earlier version used 199, the end of the 170-199 variant. Cliopatria's shape shows no such loss before the end. Confidence 1.

region.text: the whole kingdom, held to its end: Cliopatria's 215 shape plus the Krishna-Guntur coast and Banavasi

ledger.note: c. 224 CE: the Satavahana empire fragments. 'After the death of Pulumavi IV, the Satavahana empire fragmented into five smaller kingdoms': a collateral branch in the north, the Abhiras around Nashik, the Andhra Ikshvakus in the Krishna-Guntur region, the Chutus of Banavasi in northern Karnataka and the Pallavas in the south-east. Infobox 'c. 224 CE'; text 'until c. 225'; Cliopatria 223. The region is the corrected 215 shape, which now holds the lands of the successors andhra-ikshvaku (Guntur, Vijayawada) and chutu-dynasty (Banavasi).

wars.name: Kharavela's expedition against Satakarni
wars.outcome: Inconclusive in the sources: in his year 2 Kharavela 'dispatched a large army ... towards the western regions' against Satakarni, reaching 'the banks of the Krishnabena river'; scholars read it as a threat, a tribute arrangement or a friendly act.
wars.note: The years are the Cliopatria Mahameghavahana row (-170..-165); the page puts Kharavela in '2nd or 1st century BC' (Daniélou 180-130 BCE; others in the 1st century BCE or CE). The Satakarni I page quotes 'in the second year (he), disregarding Satakamini'. No border changed.

wars.name: Gautamiputra Satakarni's war on the Kshaharatas

zones.text: the Nashik and Pune country, Nahapana's Nasik and Karle inscriptions

wars.outcome: Satavahana victory: Nahapana's 'Khakharata' family 'rooted out' (Nashik inscription) and his coins restruck at Jogalthembi.
wars.note: The year is Dhavalikar's c. 124 CE (18th regnal year); Fynes says after 71 CE and Bhandare 78 CE. The Nahapana page dates Nahapana's own inscriptions by an era whose start gives 119-124 CE and also quotes 24-70 CE (Sagar) and 66-71 CE (Fynes); the Satavahana page says the Kshatrapas held the former Satavahana territory 'c. 15-40 CE'. These do not agree; none of the zone is drawn as contested.

wars.name: Rudradaman's wars with Satakarni

zones.text: the territories Nahapana had held, except Poona and Nasik; Aparanta

wars.outcome: Rudradaman 'twice in fair fight completely defeated Satakarni' (the Junagadh inscription, dated 150 CE) but spared him through their marriage tie; he regained Nahapana's former lands; Aparanta passed back as dowry.
wars.note: Rudradaman r. 130-150 on the page; which Satakarni is meant (Gautamiputra, Vasishthiputra Pulumavi or Shivaskanda) is disputed. The years are the reign, not battle dates.

wars.name: Yajna Sri Satakarni's recovery from the Western Satraps

zones.text: Aparanta and the eastern Central Provinces

wars.outcome: Yajna 'defeated the Western Satraps and reconquered their southern regions in western and central India'.
wars.note: The page dates the reign variously (c. 152-203 CE) and gives no date for the campaign; 184 is Cliopatria's year.

certainty.note: No treaty or survey frontier is dated; the pages name provinces (aharas such as Govardhana) and inscription findspots, not lines. The Pune-Nashik frontier with the Kshatrapas swung several times and is the least certain.

notes:
Cliopatria row Satavahana Dynasty -225..223, 15 shapes. Nine pages opened (budget 9). The infobox gives no area, so no area ratio could be computed.

Not settled:
1. The start. The page: scholars date the start of rule anywhere from 271 BCE to 30 BCE, the mainstream view being 'the late 2nd century BCE'. The dossier keeps Cliopatria's -225 (found at confidence 1) because the maurya-empire dossier (sa-02-a) hands the Deccan to this state at -225. If a later reviewer follows the mainstream view, the -225..-92 shapes should be dropped or reduced to a western-Deccan core (Pratishthana, Junnar, Nashik) until Kanha (c. 100-70 BCE).
2. Cliopatria's early shapes already reach Nashik, the Narmada, Vidarbha and the west coast, which the Satavahana page credits to Kanha, Satakarni I and II and Gautamiputra, so the -225..-27 shapes are an upper bound. After the sa-02-b repair the ledger carries the Malwa conquests at Cliopatria's years (-31 Ujjain, -28 Vidisha with the Kanvas), because the pages' dates (Satakarni I 70-60 BCE; Ollett 88-42 BCE for a single Satakarni) cannot be placed on the map: Ujjain is in no Satavahana, Shunga or Kanva shape before -31 and the Indo-Scythians page has Vikrama retake it in 58 BCE. The -31 shape also moves the south edge to 13.5N (Bellary, Anantapur, Dharwad) while the Satavahana page says Pulumavi 'is believed to have added the Bellary region'; left as Cliopatria draws it.
3. The Kshatrapa episode cannot be dated: the Satavahana page says the Western Kshatrapas held 'the former Satavahana territory' during 15-40 CE; the Nahapana page dates Nahapana 24-70, 66-71, to 78, or 119-124 CE; Gautamiputra's own dates run 60-85 to 106-130 CE. The Western Satraps page dates a Kshatrapa defeat of the Satavahanas to 105-106 CE (Nasik Cave 10) without naming land. No loss to Nahapana is entered (disagreement with the reviewer's second option, kept at his first: the 124 gain is confidence 1 and says it repeats land Cliopatria never removed): a loss at 105/106 would mean choosing among chronologies the pages do not choose, and Cliopatria draws 106-126 as Gautamiputra's maximum. If a later reviewer prefers the dated loss: Konkan, Malwa, Nasik and Pune would leave keyframes -27 and 106 for 105-123 and the 124 gain would become real.
4. Odisha: the -164..-50 shapes are corrected to remove Odisha (about 50,000 km2 of the shape), since the Kharavela page puts Kalinga under the Mahameghavahana; Cliopatria's +83,000 km2 at -164 is therefore not carried as a gain. Chhattisgarh (South Kosala) is now removed from the -27 and 106 shapes until 109 and regained at 110 from mahameghavahana-dynasty (sa-02-b repair); the Mahameghavahana page also says the Satavahanas kept it 'up to the second half of the 2nd century CE' and that the Meghas then 'regained their suzerainty over South Kosala' (2nd-3rd century, no year), so the shapes 161-215 that keep Chhattisgarh are probably too large; no year is given, so no loss is entered (gap).
5. Successor slugs abhira-dynasty, andhra-ikshvaku and chutu-dynasty need dossiers from another group; the northern successor ('a collateral branch') has no name on the page.
6. Gazetteer: Paithan, Junnar, Vidisha, Dharanikota, Kaushambi and Banavasi are not in places.jsonl (the capital coordinates are given directly; Vidisha and Banavasi are given as coordinates or via a neighbour).
Rulers are omitted: the pages give a regnal list but no two scholars agree on the years.
7. Sa-02-b repair (2026-10-19), what changed: Krishna-Guntur coast added to the -31..215 keyframes and the 224 dissolve (and Banavasi to 184-215); Malwa gains moved to -31 (Ujjain, counterpart nobody) and -28 (Vidisha, with the Kanvas), the -50 entry dropped; Chhattisgarh removed until 109 with a 110 gain; Nasik added to the 127 shape; Vidarbha removed from the 124 gain, now confidence 1; the Abhira loss moved from 199 to 203. Unchanged for lack of a page: the start year; the year of the Aparanta dowry (the Vashishtiputra page has none); the year of Yajna Sri's recovery; the small shape changes at -144, -66, -50, 161, 207 and 215 (none of the pages opened dates them: the Western Satraps page gives no frontier years for these).
